extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students in philosophy of humour, aesthetics, and literary studies
extracted.subtask_description: A scholarly defence and refinement of Noël Carroll's formal incongruity theory of humour, arguing against vagueness criticisms and proposing a 'pertinence' condition; illustrated by piecemeal literary analyses. Targets conceptual criteria for when an incongruity counts as comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity claim: perception of an incongruity
rubrics_metrics.description: The key claim of incongruity theory is that the perception of an incongruity is necessary for comic amusement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes standard counterexamples (caricatures, imitations, repetitions) offered against necessity but treats this as one of the central evaluative claims to be tested against instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal definition of incongruity (Carroll)
rubrics_metrics.description: An incongruity is a comparative/discordant relation: something is discordant with something else — with respect to comic amusement, that 'something else' is how the world is or should be; incongruity is a violation of general norms and expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this formal notion to identify (i) the pattern(s) of norms or expectations and (ii) the element(s) that infringe them. The author uses it to capture similarities and differences across comic texts by identifying which norms are breached.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carroll's sufficiency condition — perceived as non‑threatening / not anxiety‑producing
rubrics_metrics.description: For an incongruity to yield comic amusement, it must be perceived 'as non-threatening or otherwise anxiety producing'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This condition is intended to exclude horror or disturbing incongruities (e.g., those that produce fear rather than laughter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Carroll's sufficiency condition — not 'annoying'
rubrics_metrics.description: An incongruity should not be perceived as 'annoying' for it to be comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a person discovering they wear two different socks may be disturbed/annoyed rather than amused; such an incongruity is excluded by this condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carroll's sufficiency condition — should not 'enlist genuine problem‑solving attitudes'
rubrics_metrics.description: Incongruities that invite a problem‑solving attitude (e.g., riddles or puzzles) are not the kinds of incongruities that yield comic amusement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This excludes instances where enjoyment derives from solving and dispelling the incongruity; such cases lead to puzzlement or intellectual solution rather than levity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carroll's sufficiency condition — enjoyment of the pertinent incongruity and experience of levity
rubrics_metrics.description: The incongruity should 'give rise to the enjoyment of precisely the pertinent incongruity' and to 'an experience of levity'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ties the perception of incongruity to a specific pleasurable response (levity) focused on the pertinent incongruity rather than other reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vagueness criticism (version 1): vacuous/uninformative
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism that Carroll's articulation of incongruity is vacuous — too general or redundant to tell us what counts as an incongruity (i.e., uninformative about the object of comic amusement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author rejects this by demonstrating that even a broad formal notion can be informative when applied: one must indicate the norms/expectations and the specific violating element to illuminate the comic instance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vagueness criticism (version 2): shoehorning / unfalsifiability
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism that Carroll's vagueness allows one to 'shoehorn' an incongruity into any example (for any item i one can fabricate a violating norm ii), making the theory unfalsifiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To answer this, one needs constraints or additional conditions (the article proposes the pertinence condition) that prevent arbitrary fits and render the theory falsifiable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vagueness criticism (version 3): open‑ended / indefinitely extended
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism aimed at extended/long lists of incongruity types (e.g., 'and so forth') making the notion indeterminate and open‑ended (ascribed to McGhee/Latta).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes Carroll's formal notion is not liable to this specific complaint but raises it as another form of vagueness faced by other articulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cochrane's amendment: restrict to intentional, rule‑based norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Cochrane proposes narrowing incongruity to violations of rule‑based norms (how something ought to be) and to norms related to intentional actions/attitudes, excluding statistical, teleological and purely physical laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This avoids shoehorning but is argued to be too restrictive: many comic instances (e.g., Wile E. Coyote's defiance of gravity; teleological violations; statistical running gags) are plausibly comic even when non‑intentional or statistical norms are violated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pertinence condition (Bariselli): norms/elements must be part of same context
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendment requiring that the elements generating an incongruity are pertinent to, or part of, the same context: the norms/expectations violated must be relevant to the context of the violating element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This preserves Carroll's flexibility about what norms count while preventing arbitrary shoehorning. Examples: Three Stooges gags (everyday norms about inanimate objects are pertinent → comic) vs Beauty and the Beast (those norms are not pertinent in a fantasy world → fantastical, not comic); Beckett passages where narration‑rules are or are not pertinent determine comic vs estranging effect. Also makes the theory falsifiable: find a comic case that depends on non‑pertinent norms to falsify it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application method: piecemeal analysis of breached expectations/norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the notion of incongruity to many cases through close/piecemeal analysis, identifying which expectations or norms are breached to individuate similarities and differences of comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated with literary examples (Beckett, Sterne, Sterne vs Beckett comparisons) showing how specifying which norms are infringed explains distinct comic styles and effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for establishing pertinence: provide convincing contextual interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: When invoking the pertinence condition, one must justify why certain norms are pertinent (i.e., determine the relevant context by argument), rather than arbitrarily adjusting context to force an explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper argues that determining context may require disputable interpretations but these must be supported (e.g., in Three Stooges scenes objects are mostly inanimate outside the gag, supporting everyday‑norm pertinence; in Beauty and the Beast objects habitually animate, so the everyday norm is not pertinent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pertinence to respond to sufficiency counterexamples (surrealist, fantastical, metafictional cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pertinence functions as a non‑circular tool to handle counterexamples to Carroll's sufficiency conditions (cases that meet Carroll's conditions yet are not comic e.g., Beckett's estranging passages, Miró paintings, some surrealist works).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By showing the relevant norms are not pertinent to the work's context (e.g., immersion into an alternate dimension or recording of narrative‑forming process), the pertinence condition explains why similar incongruities produce estrangement or aesthetic enjoyment rather than comic amusement.
